As of 159 PM EST Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Mostly dry and warm weather continues across the region 
this afternoon, with high temperatures generally in the 50s to low 
60s across the area. Plenty of cloud cover associate with the 
coastal low tracking along the East Coast continues to blanket the 
region, with the cloud cover overnight helping keep temperatures on 
the mild side. As with the last few forecast cycles, the 
precipitation continues to shift further eastward, with nearly all 
of the rain missing our forecast area. Once the coastal low shifts 
eastward tonight into Monday, a sharp cold front looks to move 
through the region. A few showers may develop along the boundary, 
particularly towards the international border and higher terrain, 
although any rainfall amounts will be minimal.  

Behind the front, brisk northwest winds will follow as a strong high 
looks to build into the region. These winds will usher in colder 
temperatures  late Monday into Tuesday. High temperatures on Tuesday 
look to only climb into the 30s, nearly 20 to 25 degrees colder than 
the previous day. The brisk northwesterly flow will continue to make 
it feel quite blustery, with apparent temperatures in the 20s to low 
30s on Tuesday, quite the drastic difference from the temperatures 
in the 50s and 60s this weekend. Seasonably cool temperatures around 
5-10 degrees below normal will hang around through Wednesday, and 
winds will subside during the day on Tuesday as a large near 1040mb 
surface high sets up overhead. Under the influence of the building 
high pressure, dry conditions are expected for the start of next 
week, with no impactful weather currently expected Tuesday or 
Wednesday for any holiday travel plans.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A low pressure system looks to develop over the Gulf and 
Florida Wednesday, tracking up the Eastern Seaboard and into our 
region the night of Thanksgiving through Friday. Even though plenty 
of uncertainty remains, a few things have become clear by this 
point. The preceding airmass has continued to trend warmer, 
especially in the 900-600 mb range, with temperatures there now 
expected to stay above freezing.  Therefore, any snow from the main 
event is very unlikely. It also looks like the full warm sector will 
not reach the region, so the precipitation will mostly fall as a 
relatively cold rain, with temperatures in the 30s and 40s. At the 
onset, there will be a very dry airmass, so there will be 
significant wet-bulb cooling. The coldest air looks to be in the 
1,000-3,000 ft range and soundings show that this layer should fall 
below freezing in places at the onset of the precipitation. 
Therefore, a period of sleet and freezing rain is possible at this 
elevation for the first couple hours, even if temperatures before 
the precip are well above freezing. Because the surface low will be 
to the south, northerly winds look to persist at the surface well 
into the storm for many areas and prevent efficient surface warm-air 
advection despite strong southeasterly winds aloft. There is also a 
threat for strong winds. A strong southeasterly/easterly low-level 
jet will move overhead, with 60-70 KT likely at around the summit 
level.  

The most likely scenario, favored by most ensemble guidance and 
deterministic Euro, brings the center of the low either up the I-95 
corridor or just off the coast, heading into the Canadian Maritimes. 
While this is a slightly colder track, the airmass in place is still 
warm so it will not bring snow. However, it will likely cause more 
of an easterly component in the low-level jet and keep temperatures 
aloft slightly colder, and the sleet/freezing rain could linger 
slightly longer in the higher elevations. Overall, with warm surface 
temperatures going into it and wintry precipitation most likely at 
higher elevations, the impacts look relatively minimal at this 
point. This would also lessen any wind impacts. Soundings suggest an 
easterly track should keep the low-level jet higher up, and any 
strong winds mostly limited to the summits. 

There are still two less likely alternate scenarios. A more westerly 
track could send the low overhead, and enough surface warm-air 
advection would likely change any sleet/freezing rain from wet-
bulbing almost immediately to rain. Looking at models with this 
solution, the low-level jet looks to drop a bit lower, especially 
for southern Vermont. For example, the 06Z GFS that held this 
scenario brings the jet down to around 2500 ft near Rutland, and 
some of it below the inversion. This would cause a risk for strong 
downslope winds for some of the western slopes of the southern 
Greens. The last scenario, very unlikely but still in play, is a 
weaker low out to sea. This would allow the weak northern stream low 
over the Great Lakes to have more say, eliminating the wind threat 
and increasing warm-air advection, preventing wintry precip 
anywhere.
